title: No. 36 — The Same Subject Continued (Concerning the General Power of Taxation) (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The previous number was devoted mainly to one set of observations, and their result, as we have seen, is this. The different interests and views of the various classes of the community will naturally operate in such a way that the representatives of the people, whether they are fewer or more numerous, will be almost entirely landowners, merchants and members of the learned professions. These men will truly represent all those interests and views. Someone may object that other kinds of men have sat in the local legislatures. My answer is that I admit there are exceptions to the rule, but there are too few of them to change the general complexion or character of the government. Strong minds appear in every walk of life and rise above the disadvantages of their situation. They earn the tribute their merit deserves, not only from the classes they belong to but from society as a whole. The door ought to be equally open to everyone. I trust, for the credit of human nature, that we shall see such vigorous plants flourish in the soil of federal legislation as well as of State legislation. But a few cases of this sort do not make the reasoning any less conclusive, since it rests on the general course of things.

The subject could be placed in several other lights, and all would lead to the same result. For instance, one might ask what closer affinity or relation of interest can be imagined between the carpenter and the blacksmith, on the one hand, and the linen manufacturer or stocking weaver, on the other, than between the merchant and any of them. Everyone knows that the different branches of the mechanic or manufacturing arts are often as much rivals as any of the departments of labor and industry are. So unless the representative body were made far larger than any sound idea of order or wisdom in its deliberations would allow, the spirit of this objection, as it seems to be, could never be realized in practice. But I will say no more on a matter that has so far worn too loose a garb for anyone to inspect its real shape or tendency accurately.

Another objection, somewhat more precise, deserves our attention. It is asserted that the national legislature could never use a power of internal taxation to good effect, for two reasons: it would lack sufficient knowledge of local circumstances, and the revenue laws of the Union would interfere with those of the individual States. The claim that proper knowledge would be lacking seems to me to have no foundation at all. Suppose a State legislature is deciding a question about one of its counties that calls for knowledge of local details. How does it get that knowledge? Surely from the members who come from that county. Cannot the national legislature obtain the same knowledge from the representatives of each State? And should we not presume that the men generally sent there will be intelligent enough to pass that information along? What is knowledge of local circumstances, as applied to taxation? Is it a detailed topographical acquaintance with every mountain, river, stream, highway and bypath in each State? Or is it a general acquaintance with the State's situation and resources: the condition of its agriculture, commerce and manufactures, the nature of what it produces and consumes, and the different degrees and kinds of its wealth, property and industry?

Even under the more popular kinds of government, nations in general hand the management of their finances to single men or to small boards. These men work out and prepare the plans of taxation first, and the sovereign or the legislature afterward enacts them into law.

Everywhere, then, inquisitive and enlightened statesmen are thought best qualified to choose wisely the objects suited to revenue. As far as the opinion of mankind can count in this question, that is a clear sign of what kind of knowledge of local circumstances taxation requires.

The taxes meant by the general name of internal taxes can be divided into DIRECT and INDIRECT taxes. The objection is made against both, but its reasoning seems to be aimed only at the first. As for the second, which must be taken to mean duties and excises on articles of consumption, one cannot imagine what difficulties are feared. The knowledge needed about them must plainly be of a sort that the nature of the article itself will suggest, or that any well-informed man, especially one of the mercantile class, can easily supply. Whatever distinguishes an article's situation in one State from its situation in another must be few, simple and easy to grasp. The main thing to attend to would be to avoid articles already reserved for the use of a particular State, and there could be no trouble in finding out the revenue system of each. It could always be learned from their codes of laws, and from the members who represent the individual States.

Applied to real property, meaning houses and lands, the objection appears at first sight to have more force. Yet even here it will not survive a close look. Land taxes are commonly laid in one of two ways. One is by ACTUAL valuations, permanent or periodic. The other is by OCCASIONAL assessments, made at the discretion, or according to the best judgment, of certain officers whose duty it is to make them. In either case the EXECUTION of the business is the only part that requires knowledge of local details, and it must fall to discreet persons acting as commissioners or assessors, whether elected by the people or appointed by the government for that purpose. All the law can do is name those persons, or set out how they are to be elected or appointed, fix their numbers and qualifications, and sketch the general outlines of their powers and duties. What is there in all this that the national legislature cannot do as well as a State legislature? The attention of either can reach only general principles. As I have said, local details must be left to those who are to carry out the plan.

There is, however, a simple way of putting this matter that must be entirely satisfactory. The national legislature can use the SYSTEM OF EACH STATE WITHIN THAT STATE. The federal government can adopt and employ, in every part, the method that each State uses to lay and collect this kind of tax.

Remember also that the share of these taxes is not left to the discretion of the national legislature. It is to be fixed by the numbers of each State, as described in the second section of the first article. An actual census, or enumeration of the people, must supply the rule, and this effectively shuts the door on bias and oppression. The abuse of this power of taxation seems to have been guarded against with careful circumspection. Besides the precaution just mentioned, there is a provision that "all duties, imposts, and excises shall be UNIFORM throughout the United States."

Various speakers and writers on the side of the Constitution have rightly pointed out that if the exercise of the power of internal taxation by the Union should prove on experiment to be really inconvenient, the federal government may then give up the use of it and go back to requisitions, the formal requests to the States for money. To this, opponents have triumphantly replied: why not leave out that ambiguous power in the first place and depend on the other resource? Two solid answers can be given. First, if the power turns out to be convenient, it will be preferable because it will be more effective, and no theory can prove, nor anything but experiment, that it cannot be used to advantage. Indeed the opposite seems most probable. Second, simply having such a power in the Constitution will give requisitions a strong influence. When the States know that the Union can act without their help, they will have a powerful motive to make an effort themselves.

Next, the objection that the revenue laws of the Union and of its members will interfere. We have already seen that their authorities cannot clash or conflict. In a legal sense, then, the laws cannot interfere with each other. And it is far from impossible to avoid interference even in the policy of their different systems. An effective means is for each side to keep away from the objects that the other has taken up first. Neither can CONTROL the other, so each will plainly and sensibly see that it has an interest in this mutual restraint. Where there is an IMMEDIATE common interest, we may safely count on its working. Once the particular debts of the States are cleared away and their expenses are held within their natural limits, hardly any possibility of interference will remain. A small land tax will meet the needs of the States, and will be their simplest and most fitting resource.

Many specters have been conjured out of this power of internal taxation to alarm the people. We have heard of double sets of revenue officers, of burdens doubled by double taxation, and of the frightful shapes of odious and oppressive poll taxes. All of these have been played upon with the ingenious dexterity of political sleight of hand.

Take the first point. There are two cases in which there can be no room for double sets of officers. In the first, the right to impose the tax belongs exclusively to the Union, as with duties on imports. In the second, the object has not yet come under any State regulation or provision, which may be true of a variety of objects. In other cases, the United States will probably either stay away entirely from objects already taken up for local purposes, or use State officers and State regulations to collect the additional charge. This will best serve the aims of revenue, since it saves the expense of collection, and it will best avoid giving the State governments and the people any occasion for disgust. At all events, here is a workable way to avoid such a problem, and nothing more is required than to show that the evils predicted do not necessarily follow from the plan.

Next, any argument drawn from a supposed system of influence. It is enough to answer that such a thing ought not to be presumed. But the supposition also admits of a more precise answer. Suppose such a spirit did infest the councils of the Union. The surest road to its goal would be to employ the State officers as much as possible, and to bind them to the Union by adding to their pay. That would turn the tide of State influence into the channels of the national government, instead of making federal influence run in an opposite and hostile current. But all suppositions of this kind are invidious and ought to be kept out of the great question before the people. They serve no purpose except to cast a mist over the truth.

The suggestion of double taxation has a plain answer. The wants of the Union must be supplied one way or another. If they are supplied by the authority of the federal government, they will not be supplied by the State governments. The total amount of taxes the community pays must be the same either way. There is, however, an advantage if the Union makes the provision. The chief resource of commercial imposts, the most convenient branch of revenue, can be prudently developed much further under federal than under State regulation, which will naturally make it less necessary to turn to more inconvenient methods. There is a further advantage. To whatever extent the power of internal taxation really is difficult to exercise, that very difficulty will encourage greater care in choosing and arranging the means. It must naturally make it a fixed point of policy in the national administration to go as far as practicable in making the luxury of the rich pay into the public treasury, so as to lessen the need for impositions that might create dissatisfaction among the poorer and most numerous classes of society. How fortunate when the interest that a government has in preserving its own power coincides with a proper distribution of the public burdens, and tends to protect the least wealthy part of the community from oppression!

As for poll taxes, I confess without hesitation that I disapprove of them. They have prevailed from an early period in those States(1) that have always been the most tenacious of their rights. Even so, I should be sorry to see them introduced under the national government. But does it follow that, because a power to lay them exists, they will actually be laid? Every State in the Union has the power to impose taxes of this kind, and yet in several of them they are unknown in practice. Are the State governments to be stigmatized as tyrannies because they hold this power? If they are not, how can the same power justify such a charge against the national government, or even be urged as an obstacle to adopting it? However unfriendly I am to this kind of imposition, I am still thoroughly convinced that the federal government ought to have the power of resorting to it. Nations face certain emergencies in which expedients that should be avoided in the ordinary state of things become essential to the public welfare. Because such emergencies are possible, the government ought always to have the option of using them. The real scarcity in this country of objects that can be counted on as productive sources of revenue is a reason peculiar to ourselves for not limiting the discretion of the national councils in this respect. There may be critical and tempestuous conjunctures of the State in which a poll tax becomes an invaluable resource. And since I know nothing that exempts this part of the globe from the common calamities that have befallen other parts, I confess my aversion to any scheme that would disarm the government of even one weapon that might, in any possible contingency, be usefully employed for the general defense and security.

(I have now finished examining those of the powers proposed for the United States that bear directly on the energy of the government, and I have tried to answer the principal objections made against them. I have said nothing of the minor authorities, which are either too inconsiderable to have been thought worth the hostility of the opponents of the Constitution, or so obviously proper that they admit of no dispute. The mass of judiciary power, however, might have claimed an investigation under this head. I decided against it because its organization and its extent can be considered more advantageously together, and so I refer it to the next branch of our inquiries.)(E1)

(I have now finished examining those powers proposed for the federal government that relate more particularly to its energy and to its effectiveness in achieving the great and primary objects of union. There are others which I have omitted here, but which will be taken up under the next head of our inquiries, to make the view of the subject more complete. I flatter myself that the progress made so far will have satisfied the fair and judicious part of the community of this: some of the objections most strenuously urged against the Constitution, and most formidable when they first appeared, are not only without substance but, had they influenced the framing of the plan, would have made it unfit for the great ends of public happiness and national prosperity. I flatter myself equally that a further and more critical investigation of the system will recommend it still more to every sincere and disinterested advocate of good government, and will leave men of this character no doubt of the propriety and expediency of adopting it. How fortunate it will be for ourselves, and how much more honorable for human nature, if we have wisdom and virtue enough to set so glorious an example to mankind!)(E1)
1. The New England States.
E1. Two versions of this paragraph appear in different editions.
